title: Who is behind it
standfirst: Age, ownership and what happens when the service breaks. This is the part of a sandbox that no amount of documentation testing can tell you.
idea: A sandbox is a dependency. Your agent's files, its logins and sometimes its only copy of a working environment live on someone else's machine. The company behind it decides how long that machine is likely to exist, who owns it after an acquisition, and whether anyone answers when it fails.

Three signals are public and useful: how old the product is, whether it has changed hands, and whether there is a status page with a history. A status page that shows a real incident is more reassuring than one that is permanently green.

An SLA is a promise with a remedy. Several providers here publish none, and one publishes a promise its status page was not meeting during research. That is not a reason to avoid it; it is a reason to know it.

splits.heading: Age and ownership
body: Boat, Agent 37 and Sandboxer are weeks or months old. Runtime's public repository was created in late September 2026. boxd raised a €2M pre-seed in September 2026. InstaBox is part of InsForge, a YC P26 company.

Blaxel is the only acquisition in the set: Baseten acquired it on 10 September 2026 and says the product continues. Lizard's funding and headcount are not published. Morph's company details are not published at all.

splits.heading: Status pages and SLAs
body: Agent 37, Boat, Lizard, Runtime, Sandboxer and Vercel publish status pages. boxd and InstaBox do not have a working one. Morph and Sprites have no Sprite-specific status page established.

Only some publish an SLA. Boat claims 99.95% measured sandbox uptime; Runtime promises 99% monthly and its status page showed 96.37% over seven days at the time of research. InstaBox puts a 99.9% SLA on Enterprise.

splits.heading: What an acquisition changes
body: Blaxel's terms page predates the acquisition, and its Baseten-managed workspaces have a documented offboarding gap: removing a user from Baseten does not delete their Blaxel identity. Those are ordinary integration seams, not signs of closure, but they are the details a buyer should know.

For the rest, the honest answer is that the research records what is published and nothing more. A missing company page is not evidence of instability, and a funding round is not evidence of permanence.

watchFor: How old the product is, and whether the company page exists at all.
Whether it has been acquired, and whether the product is still shipping.
Whether there is a status page with incident history.
Whether an SLA exists, and what remedy it offers.
Whether the contracting entity and terms match the brand.
